summary:
Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law, care access and marriage are set nationally and apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors. What is specific to the region is where recorded anti-LGBT+ offending falls and how the Paris agglomeration's LGBT venues and events are policed.

The Interior Ministry's statistics service (SSMSI), in Infraction rapide n°53 of May 2025, records 4,800 anti-LGBT+ offences across France in 2024, up 5% on 2023, with crimes and délicts up 14% per year since 2016. Only about 4% of victims file a complaint, so the recorded figure understates incidence. Acts concentrate in urban units of more than 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris, where the recorded rate is 22 offences per 100,000 against a national rate of 7; the note attributes part of the Paris figure to non-resident victims and commuters. Recorded victims are more than 70% men.

Paris Pride (the Marche des fiertés) of 28 June 2025 was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry, according to franceinfo. CRS police reinforcements were deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march, with police positioned to separate the opposing groups. Large LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration therefore carry a documented far-right counter-presence alongside a heavy security response.

Paris holds France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure, including the country's only officially organised gaybourhoods and the annual Pride parade. As of 2004 the city had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops. The city also carries a documented targeted-violence history: Bertrand Delanoë, who became France's first openly gay mayor of Paris in 2002, was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals. The most recent documented targeted-violence incident in this record is that 2002 stabbing; no later instance against a public LGBT figure in Paris is documented here.
tangentialFactors:
The Paris offending rate of 22 per 100,000 (2024) sits above the national rate of 7, but the source itself notes the gap is partly an artefact of non-resident victims and commuters being counted against the Paris unit, so the figure should not be read as a clean per-resident risk rate. The counts are raw, with no denominator for the size of the LGBT population supplied.

The 4% complaint rate means recorded offending is a fraction of reported experience; direction of travel (up 5% in 2024, crimes/délicts up 14% annually since 2016) is more informative than the level.

Paris's unusually dense LGBT venue infrastructure cuts both ways: it supports ordinary social movement for a trans visitor, and it concentrates the counter-presence and policing seen at the 28 June 2025 Pride.
localsOnly:
Residents of Île-de-France live under the national legal baseline: anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation since 1985 and gender identity since 2012; legal gender change without surgery or medical diagnosis since 2017; declassification of gender dysphoria as a mental illness in 2010; PACS from 1999 and marriage equality from 2013.

Complaint behaviour is a local fact: only about 4% of anti-LGBT+ victims file a complaint (SSMSI, May 2025), and recorded victims are more than 70% men, indicating that women's and trans-specific experiences are under-captured in the official counts.

Local LGBT civic life includes France's only officially organised gaybourhoods and the annual Pride parade, both of which now sit inside a security cordon when classified a sensitive event, as on 28 June 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory supplies no Île-de-France-specific data on detention placement, border or airport screening of trans travellers, document-marker handling, facilities access, or care provision within the region; those layers are carried by the national record and are not sourced here at region level.

The Paris offending rate's attribution to non-resident victims and commuters is the source's own partial explanation; the residual portion attributable to residents is not quantified and remains unresolved.

No figure in the inventory isolates trans-specific offending within the anti-LGBT+ totals for Île-de-France; the recorded-victim breakdown is by sex, not gender identity.

The 140-venue count for Paris is dated 2004 and no later count is supplied, so current venue density is not sourced.
